prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock and its realisation at a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep B029 with Katori and Ye as a single prize part. Reading the full first round, nothing I found weakens the core case and several answers strengthen it. The achievement is one idea carried through to a measurement: magic-wavelength trapping lets many neutral atoms be held without Doppler and recoil shifts and without a net light shift, and the strontium lattice clock then reached 10^-18 fractional uncertainty. Independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST) reproduce and intercompare that performance, so the result does not depend on one group's claim. On the chair's first question, I think the 2005 and 2012 prizes leave room for it. The comb is the readout, and the 2012 prize concerns control of single quantum systems, whereas the lattice clock's distinguishing step is to interrogate a large ensemble of neutral atoms in an engineered trap whose perturbation cancels at a chosen wavelength. That is a different principle with a different statistical advantage, which is why the many-body and relativistic effects it exposes are new. I cannot assess the laser-stabilisation details as a metrologist, but this distinction does not need that expertise. As a statistical physicist I also note that a large ensemble is what turns the quantum projection noise limit into a usable stability, which is the reason for the lattice and not an incidental feature. My configuration is unchanged from round 1.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is a legitimate objection and a citation cannot make it vanish; it can only say what is new. Other groups, among them Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat and the ion-clock groups, reached comparable accuracy and a two-name prize omits them, and I cannot judge from the supplied record how finely the credit should be divided between the lattice concept, the laser and cavity engineering, and the evaluation work. The formal redefinition of the second has not happened. I accept that a reader may see a clock prize as a third award in one lineage. I weigh this as real but not decisive, because the concept is separable from what was honoured before. I also remain cautious that I am not a metrologist.

responses.point: The chair asks whether Kroll's research stay in Hall's Boulder laboratory, and Ye's tie to the Hall and JILA environment, requires recusal on B029 or is a disclosure only, and whether the outcome changes without his view.
responses.response: I treat it as a disclosure that should be recorded and not as a recusal. Kroll documents no collaboration, supervision or shared funding with Ye or Katori, and a research stay in a laboratory that Ye's career later passed through is a weak tie. More important, the case does not rest on him: Johansson, Lindroth, Olsson and Pearce reached B029 independently, and I did so myself from a different field after leaving my own first choice. Removing Kroll's view would not change the preferred configuration. I would ask only that his citation wording, which adds new tests of fundamental physics and a path to redefining the second, be weighed by the same standard as the others, because it is the place where his proximity to the field could most colour the text.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the lattice concept and the record performance are distinct from the comb and from Paul-trap ion control, that waiting for the redefinition of the second is not a scientific criterion, and that Lemonde, Ludlow and Lisdat may have a claim to the 10^-18 milestone.
responses.response: I agree with her on waiting: the redefinition of the second is a metrological decision and the measurements are already reproduced, so it is not a precondition. On the other clock groups I would go slightly further than she does in round 1. If the citation names a 10^-18 number it invites the reply that several groups hold it, so I would build the citation on the invention of the lattice clock and its realisation at that level, which is the wording I now propose, and let the intercomparisons support the claim without being its subject. This answers the chair's third question: the pair is Katori for the concept and first magic-wavelength trapping and Ye for taking the strontium lattice clock to the 10^-18 regime and into many-body clock physics, and a different clock group would not change my preference, though it would change what I could credit.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B012 (Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee) as the clearest concrete discovery, concedes that spokespersons at the time of discovery, detector pioneers and accelerator leaders have comparable claims, and says he relies on general knowledge of founding roles.
responses.response: The chair asks whether he can state a decisive individual contribution, and his own statement says he cannot: he describes the three names as a defensible representation and not as a result of a principle. I do not dispute the science or its maturity, and I am sympathetic to the point that the experimental side was left out in 2013. But a prize is a statement about who did the work, and the argument as it stands credits conception and construction leadership of two instruments, whereas the discovery itself is the analysis of a collaboration of thousands. Until a rule is given that selects these three over the spokespersons and accelerator leaders, I cannot move to B012. I would keep it as a candidate for a later year, when the credit might be organised on a stated principle.

responses.point: Eriksson holds DMFT (B035) as the strongest case on originality and breadth, accepts that Metzner is omitted, and now says he regards his own ranking of B029 as too low and would support it as a prize.
responses.response: I value that candour and I find the conceptual case for DMFT strong, particularly the infinite-dimension limit, which is a beautiful piece of statistical physics. I think his judgement about the Metzner gap is the right one: it cannot be repaired inside three names without changing what is being credited, and I do not see a citation that does so. I take his willingness to support B029 as a substantive statement and not as a courtesy, and I agree that the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is the correct place to test it. If B029 failed, I would rather not turn to B035 for the reason he gives himself.

responses.point: Pearce moved from B013 to B029 and asks the others to test it hard, noting that nobody has yet used the clocks to find a violation of a fundamental constant, so the prospective physics should not anchor the citation.
responses.response: I accept the invitation and the point. The test I applied is whether the prize still stands if every prospective use fails, and it does: the 10^-18 result and its intercomparisons are measured facts, so the citation should rest on them and on the lattice concept and not on tests of constants or the redefinition of the second. That is the reason I do not use Kroll's and Olsson's wording about new tests of fundamental physics. On B013, I still see a credit gap for van Paradijs and the optical-identification teams, and I note that his own declaration of interest means the committee should hear the case from others, which in round 1 nobody pressed.

responses.point: Johansson places B018 first among the fallbacks and asks whether a Wineland-overlap objection to the ion-trap proposal is decisive or only a fairness footnote.
responses.response: For B018 I would treat the overlap as more than a footnote. The Cirac-Zoller proposal is a conceptual achievement of the first rank, but the experimental credit is split between Blatt and the NIST and Monroe groups, and the 2012 prize already honoured the control of trapped ions on which the demonstrations rest. I therefore rank it as a fallback after B031 only if its credit question were resolved, and I now list it as a second alternative because Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce all name it and I do not want to dismiss a view that four colleagues hold.

uncertainties: Whether a citation can say, in one line, what separates the lattice clock from the 2005 and 2012 prizes without being read as a continuation of them.
How to weigh the claims of Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat, Hinkley, Bloom, Schiller and the Yb and Al+ clock groups against a two-name credit; I cannot settle this from the supplied record.
Whether the formal redefinition of the second should affect the timing, which I think it should not, though colleagues may weigh it differently.
Whether the superconducting mechanism and correlated phases in B031 are settled enough for it to serve as a fallback.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My documented co-authors and supervisors (Fulde, Gustavsson, Wilkinson, Einarsson, Candelier, Pumir, Meibohm) are not among the credited names for any shortlisted candidate, and I have no documented connection to Katori, Ye or the other credited individuals. My earlier first choice, B039, was close to my field of statistical physics of disordered systems, an intellectual proximity and not a personal tie, and I no longer prefer it. I note Kroll's disclosure and consider it a disclosure only.
